title: Newton-Girard Identities: 400 Years from Girard to Lean 4
content: The Newton-Girard (or Newton's) identities were discovered by Albert Girard in *Invention nouvelle en l'algèbre* (1629) and independently restated by Newton around 1666 (published in *Arithmetica Universalis*, 1707). They express power sums pₖ = Σxᵢᵏ recursively in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials eₖ = Σ_{i₁<...<iₖ} xᵢ₁···xᵢₖ. The Mathlib formalization uses `MvPolynomial.psum_eq_mul_esymm_sub_sum`, which encodes the general recurrence via a filtered antidiagonal sum. This file derives the three most-used corollaries (k=1,2,3) by instantiating the general recurrence at specific degrees and computing the antidiagonal filters explicitly.
mathContext: The general Newton-Girard recurrence: $p_k = (-1)^{k+1} k\, e_k - \sum_{\substack{a+b=k \\ 0 < a < k}} (-1)^a e_a\, p_b$, where $p_k = \sum_i X_i^k$ and $e_k = \text{esymm}(\sigma, R, k)$. Mathlib encodes this as `MvPolynomial.psum_eq_mul_esymm_sub_sum` over a `[CommRing R] [Fintype σ]`.

title: Generality: Any CommRing over Any Fintype
content: The `variable` declaration fixes a `CommRing R` and a `Fintype σ`, giving the Newton-Girard corollaries in full algebraic generality. All three theorems hold over any commutative ring — not just ℝ or ℚ — with coefficients indexed by any finite type σ. This is more general than the classical statement (which usually specializes to ℝ[x₁,...,xₙ]) and directly applicable in Mathlib's MvPolynomial framework.
mathContext: $R$ is any commutative ring, $\sigma$ is any finite type (index set). The power sum $p_k = \sum_{i : \sigma} X_i^k \in R[X_1,\ldots,X_{|\sigma|}]$ and $e_k = \text{esymm}(\sigma, R, k)$ are elements of `MvPolynomial σ R`.

title: Corollary k=1: Bridging psum_one and esymm_one by Transitivity
content: The k=1 case `p₁ = e₁` follows from a one-line proof: `psum_one` states p₁ = Σ X i, and `esymm_one` states e₁ = Σ X i. These two Mathlib lemmas each individually give the same sum, so equality is proved by `.trans ... .symm` — a chain `p₁ = Σ X i = e₁` using transitivity and symmetry of equality. No unfolding or ring calculation is needed because both quantities are definitionally equal to the same Finset sum.
mathContext: $p_1 = \sum_{i : \sigma} X_i = e_1$. Formally: `(MvPolynomial.psum_one σ R).trans (MvPolynomial.esymm_one σ R).symm`. The antidiagonal for $k=1$ is empty (no $a$ with $0 < a < 1$), so the recurrence reduces to $p_1 = (-1)^2 \cdot 1 \cdot e_1 = e_1$.

title: Corollary k=2: Antidiagonal Filter {(1,1)} Yields p₂ = e₁² − 2e₂
content: The k=2 case applies `psum_eq_mul_esymm_sub_sum` at degree 2. The key step is computing the filtered antidiagonal: among pairs (a,b) with a+b=2 and 0<a<2, the only solution is (1,1). This is proved by `ext` + `simp` + `omega` — the omega tactic handles the linear arithmetic constraint `a+b=2 ∧ 0<a<2 ↔ a=1 ∧ b=1` automatically. After simplification with `simp [hfilt, h1]`, the recurrence becomes `-2·e₂ + e₁·e₁`, closed by `ring` to `e₁² − 2e₂`.
mathContext: $p_2 = (-1)^3 \cdot 2 \cdot e_2 - (-1)^1 \cdot e_1 \cdot p_1 = -2e_2 + e_1^2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2$. The antidiagonal: $\{(a,b) \mid a+b=2,\, 0 < a < 2\} = \{(1,1)\}$, so the sum has one term: $(-1)^1 e_1 \cdot p_1 = -e_1^2$ (after substituting $p_1 = e_1$).

title: Corollary k=3: Two-Element Antidiagonal {(1,2),(2,1)} Yields p₃ = e₁p₂ − e₂p₁ + 3e₃
content: The k=3 case follows the same pattern as k=2, but the antidiagonal filter now has two elements: (1,2) and (2,1), corresponding to the two terms in the recurrence. The filter `{(a,b) | a+b=3, 0<a<3}` is proved equal to `{(1,2),(2,1)}` by `ext` + `simp` + `omega`. `sum_insert` then separates the two-element sum (verifying (1,2) ∉ {(2,1)} by `decide`), and `ring` closes the resulting algebraic expression. The pattern — antidiagonal filter by omega, sum_insert to separate terms, ring to close — scales to any fixed k.
